opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think one of the most fundamental limitations is that RLHF is essentially shaping the model's outputs after the fact rather than changing how the model actually reasons. You train a large model to predict the next token, and then you use human preferences to nudge it toward responses people like. That works quite well for things like tone, helpfulness, and avoiding obviously bad outputs. But it doesn't give the model a real mechanism for checking whether its answer is correct, or for spending more effort when a problem is harder.

Human feedback is also a very noisy and limited signal. People are good at saying "I prefer this response to that one," especially for surface-level qualities, but they're much worse at evaluating long chains of reasoning, complex code, or subtle factual errors. So you end up optimizing for what *looks* good to a human rater, which isn't always what's actually right. That's where you see issues like sycophancy, or models producing very confident, fluent answers that are wrong.

And there's a scalability problem. Collecting high-quality human preferences is expensive, and as models tackle harder problems, it becomes harder for humans to give reliable feedback at all. You can't really supervise something meaningfully if you can't evaluate its outputs.

A lot of my own thinking has been about an alternative: instead of just training a policy that maps an input directly to an answer, you learn something more like a verifier, or an energy function, that scores how compatible a candidate answer is with the problem. Then generation becomes an optimization process. You can iteratively refine an answer, and for harder problems you can spend more computation searching for a better solution. That gives you a kind of built-in self-evaluation that RLHF doesn't really provide.

It also composes nicely. If you have separate models capturing different constraints or concepts, you can combine them at inference time and look for solutions that satisfy all of them, which helps you generalize to combinations you never saw in training. With RLHF, you're largely stuck with whatever the single monolithic policy learned.

So I'd say RLHF is a useful tool for alignment and polish, but it's not a substitute for models that can actually reason, verify, and adapt their computation to the difficulty of the problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the fundamental issue with RLHF is that you're essentially bottlenecked by the quality of the human judgments you're collecting. The whole pipeline assumes that a person can look at two responses and reliably tell you which one is better. And for a lot of simple tasks, that's fine. But as you push toward harder problems, like long mathematical proofs, complex code, or scientific reasoning, humans actually can't verify these things very well. So what you end up optimizing for is not correctness, but what looks correct to a person in a few seconds of reading. The model learns to be persuasive rather than right.

And the second piece, which I think is maybe more subtle, is that the reward model you train from those preferences is itself just another neural network. It's a lossy, imperfect proxy for what you actually care about. When you then run reinforcement learning against it, the policy is very good at finding the places where that proxy is wrong. So you get this reward hacking behavior, where the model exploits the gaps in the reward model instead of genuinely improving. People try to patch this with KL penalties and so on, but fundamentally you're regularizing toward the original model rather than toward truth.

So from my perspective, the more promising direction is to lean on signals that actually come from the world or from verifiable structure. Things like whether code runs, whether a proof checks, whether a prediction about a physical system matches what happens. Those don't saturate the way human preference does, and they don't drift as the model gets smarter than the annotators. RLHF is great for alignment of style and basic helpfulness, but I don't think it's the path to models that reason better than we do.

astra-6.text: I think a fundamental limitation is that human feedback is only as good as our ability to evaluate what the model is doing. If a model gives you an answer to a really difficult problem, you might not know whether that answer is correct. You might prefer it because it sounds convincing or is presented nicely. So optimizing for that preference doesn’t necessarily mean optimizing for correctness. And as we ask models to do things that go beyond human expertise, that becomes an increasingly important bottleneck: how do you provide a reliable learning signal for something you can’t reliably judge?
